item.title: Beyond the banana raft: Asadul’s story and the road to better education in chars. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
During the monsoon period, going to school was never just a simple walk for Asadul.
The books in his schoolbag often became wet. The muddy path between home and school turned slippery and treacherous. A deep canal stood between his home and the classroom, and when rain came, it swelled into a strong current.
Sometimes he waded through waist-deep water. On other days, he crossed on a raft made of banana trees.
Yet he kept going.
For a boy growing up in the remote char village of Nowshala in Kurigram's Chilmari upazila, school represented something much greater than a classroom. It was a pathway to a different life.
From an early age, Asadul dreamed of becoming a doctor -- a dream that appeared almost impossible in a place where even reaching school became a daily struggle.
Today, that boy is a student at Rangpur Medical College.
His journey is extraordinary, and it also speaks to a much larger reality in Bangladesh.
Over the past decades, the country has made significant progress in bringing children into school. About 97% of primary school-aged children were enrolled in school, while the dropout rate declined significantly from 40% in 2010 to 13% in 2023.
But, for those living in remote and climate-vulnerable areas, the harder challenge is often staying in school, completing secondary education, and finding a pathway to higher education.
Bangladesh has made steady progress in expanding access to education, but significant gaps remain in remote char areas.
The Bangladesh Education Sector Analysis 2026 highlights persistent “last mile” challenges, high dropout rates, and continuing disparities affecting children from low-income households, remote and vulnerable areas, and other marginalized groups.
Asadul's life offers a human face to those statistics.
When he was growing up, there was no school in the vicinity of Nowshala, surrounded by the Brahmaputra River. For the communities, education remained beyond reach.
That began to change in 2006, when Friendship established a primary school in the area. Asadul enrolled in 2008.
He was still young, but he had already seen the harshness of char life.
River erosion repeatedly threatened his family's home and land. Poverty was a constant reality.
Yet while the river could take away land and possessions, it could not take away his determination to study.
"During floods, I sometimes crossed the canal on a banana raft. Often my books and notebooks got wet," Asadul recalls. "But I always felt that if I stopped going to school, my dream would disappear too."
It is difficult to imagine what those words meant to a child who had to negotiate floodwater simply to attend class. But for Asadul, education had already become inseparable from his hope for a better future.
Photo of Asadul at Rangpur Medical College. Photo: Courtesy
After six years of struggle, he completed primary education. Yet the next stage proved even more difficult.
There was still no nearby secondary education opportunity. To continue studying, Asadul had to leave home and depend on others.
He stayed in different households, taught their children, and did household work in exchange for food and accommodation. He also worked in hotels, agricultural farms, and crop-processing centers.
His education was sustained not by comfort, but by sacrifice.
"To continue my studies, I had to move from one house to another. In return, I taught their children and did different kinds of work, he says."
The arrangement was not always kind.
"Sometimes families demanded money for food and accommodation, which I could not afford. I had to leave those places and start again elsewhere. There were days when I worked in other people's homes just to arrange one meal."
Still, he refused to abandon his education.
"I always carried a dream -- to become educated, change my destiny, and bring happiness to my family and society."
His daily routine was grueling: Classes during the day, work in the afternoon and evening, and study late into the night.
Eventually, he completed both secondary and higher secondary education.
Then came the medical admission test.
For Asadul, becoming a doctor had never been simply about choosing a profession. It had become a personal promise -- to himself and to the family whose hardships he had witnessed since childhood.
Guidance and encouragement from mentors helped him gain confidence about higher education and career choices. He began studying 14 to 15 hours a day.
But his first attempt at the medical admission test ended in regret. He missed the opportunity by just two marks.
For many students, such a narrow margin of failure could have ended the dream. For Asadul, it became another reason to try.
The following year, the result he had waited for finally arrived.
In the 2022–23 academic session, Asadul secured admission to Rangpur Medical College.
The distance he had travelled was not merely geographical. It was a journey from a place where a child once had to cross floodwater to reach a primary classroom to a point where that same child could enter one of the country's prominent medical colleges.
"Every night before going to sleep, I feel that I am finally becoming a doctor," he says. "In the future, I want to serve disadvantaged people as a compassionate physician."
His words carry a significance beyond personal achievement.
Bangladesh's education story is often told through enrollment figures and examination results. But behind those numbers are children whose educational journeys are shaped by where they are born, whether their families can afford to keep them in school, whether a road remains passable during the rainy season, and whether they can see a future beyond the next examination.
The challenge is particularly acute in climate-vulnerable communities.
Unicef says children living in disaster-affected parts of Bangladesh are among those most at risk of exclusion from school.
In 2024 alone, climate-related events disrupted the education of 35 million children in Bangladesh, with heatwaves, cyclones, and floods causing repeated school closures and, in some areas, children losing up to eight weeks of learning.
For children in the chars , education must mean more than opening the door of a school. It must mean creating a continuous pathway -- from primary education to secondary school, from secondary school to higher education, and eventually from education to dignified work and meaningful participation in society.
The support of educational initiatives and career guidance can help students from remote communities see possibilities that may otherwise remain invisible.
Asadul’s story is ultimately about what a young person can do when opportunity meets determination. Yet stories like his suggest that something else is changing in Bangladesh’s chars.
As access to education expands, children are beginning to imagine futures as doctors, engineers, teachers, and other professionals.
It reminds us that talent does not belong only to cities, nor does ambition stop at the edge of a river.
This is the larger promise of education in Bangladesh: Not simply getting children into classrooms, but enabling them to stay, learn, progress, and aspire.
Building a better Bangladesh therefore requires more than expanding access. It requires resilient schools and learning opportunities in vulnerable communities, stronger support for children at risk of dropping out, quality learning, pathways from primary to secondary education, career guidance, and opportunities to continue into higher education.
The boy who once crossed floodwaters on a banana raft is now on his way to becoming a doctor.
His story is not only about how far one child has travelled. It is about how far Bangladesh can take its children if education reaches the last mile and the pathway does not end there.
Sometimes, building a better future begins with simply helping a child reach school. The real transformation comes when that child is given the opportunity to keep going.
Ruhul Kuddus is the General Manager of the Education Sector, Friendship.

item.title: Ensuring remittance keeps trending upwards. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is encouraging to find that remittance inflows have reportedly increased by 18.6% to $6.05 billion in the current fiscal year, especially at a time when the country continues to navigate economic pressures and needs stronger foreign-exchange earnings.
Remittances have long been one of Bangladesh’s most dependable sources of foreign currency while also providing vital support to millions of families, so the latest growth deserves recognition.
More importantly, this should encourage policy-makers to build on the factors that are helping formal remittance channels become more attractive and accessible.
For a country with a large overseas workforce, there is considerable room to do more: Migrant workers make enormous sacrifices to earn abroad, and ensuring that their hard-earned money can be sent home safely, quickly, and at reasonable cost should be a priority.
Globally, the cost of sending remittances remains significant, with the World Bank reporting an average cost of 6.36% across the corridors it tracks, and Bangladesh must continue working to reduce such costs.
At the same time, the government and financial institutions need to maintain policies that encourage migrants to use official channels. Better exchange rates, simplified procedures, stronger digital services, and greater confidence in the banking system can help sustain the upward trend while reducing reliance on informal methods.
But increasing remittance inflows should not become an excuse for complacency. Bangladesh must ensure that these foreign earnings contribute to broader economic stability and productive investment in long-term economic security rather than merely meeting immediate consumption needs.
The latest figures are undoubtedly positive; they demonstrate the continuing contribution of Bangladeshis working overseas and offer some much-needed momentum for the economy.
Now, we must keep the focus on making formal remittance channels even easier, protecting migrant workers’ interests, and creating an environment where every dollar sent home can generate maximum value for families and the country alike.

item.title: Literacy must mean more. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As we observe International Literacy Day today, it is important to remind ourselves that literacy is not merely the ability to read and write but a fundamental human right and a foundation for accessing wider knowledge, skills, and opportunities.
Yet, it is disheartening that despite decades of progress, at least 739 million young people and adults worldwide still lack basic literacy skills.
For Bangladesh, this remains a particularly relevant concern. The country has made significant strides in expanding access to education, particularly among younger generations: Unesco data put youth literacy at 93.4%, while literacy among those aged 25-64 stands at 76.1%.
These figures show both how far Bangladesh has come and how much work still remains.
More importantly, literacy cannot be treated as a statistic that ends once someone can sign their name or read a sentence. In an increasingly digital society, people must be able to understand information, distinguish fact from misinformation, navigate technology, and also apply what they learn to everyday decisions.
This is especially important in Bangladesh, where access to digital services, financial systems, healthcare information, and government services is rapidly expanding.
The challenge here is twofold: Ensuring that children receive strong foundational literacy and reaching adults who were left behind by the formal education system.
Rural communities, disadvantaged families, older people, and those living in climate-vulnerable areas deserve particular attention.
Encouragingly, Bangladesh already has examples of innovative approaches, such as Sidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha’s solar-powered floating schools, which received Unesco’s Confucius Literacy Prize.
The government must build on such initiatives rather than treating literacy as a campaign-day issue. Better-funded adult education, stronger foundational learning, trained teachers, and accessible digital-literacy programmes are essential.
On this International Literacy Day, Bangladesh should remind itself that literacy is not simply about producing people who can read. It is about empowering citizens to understand, participate, and prosper -- and that must remain the ultimate goal.

item.title: What you can do to combat dengue. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is no longer facing dengue as a simple seasonal disease. It has evolved into a complex public health challenge influenced by climate change, rapid urbanization, environmental degradation, changing human behavior, and weaknesses in vector control systems.
The alarming rise in dengue cases over the past several years clearly indicates that traditional approaches are no longer sufficient. Dengue prevention and control must now be viewed as a national development priority rather than merely a health-sector responsibility. The changing epidemiology of dengue in Bangladesh demands a fundamental shift in strategy.
Climate change isn't just altering ecosystems but actively reshaping infectious disease boundaries and elevating the spillover and epidemic risks of neglected, rare pathogens. Climate change has significantly altered the pattern of mosquito-borne diseases worldwide, and Bangladesh is among the countries most vulnerable to its consequences.
Rising temperatures, irregular rainfall, prolonged monsoon seasons, waterlogging, floods, and increasing humidity have created ideal conditions for the breeding and survival of Aedes mosquitoes. Previously, dengue transmission was largely concentrated between June and September. However, recent outbreaks have demonstrated that the transmission season has expanded beyond traditional boundaries.
Unpredictable weather patterns are allowing mosquitoes to reproduce more rapidly and survive for longer periods. Urban flooding creates countless artificial breeding sites, while warmer temperatures accelerate both mosquito development and viral replication.
Therefore, climate change adaptation strategies must be integrated into Bangladesh's dengue control policies. Public health authorities should collaborate closely with meteorological agencies, urban planners, environmental experts, and local government institutions to develop climate-informed dengue forecasting models.
One of the greatest misconceptions in Bangladesh is the belief that fogging alone can control dengue.
Fogging primarily targets adult mosquitoes and often provides only temporary relief. However, Aedes mosquitoes reproduce in small collections of clean, stagnant water found inside homes, on rooftops, in flowerpots, in discarded containers, on construction sites, in water storage facilities, etc.
The most effective intervention remains the destruction of mosquito breeding sites. Vector control should become a year-round activity rather than an emergency response implemented only after case numbers begin to rise.
Dengue control ultimately depends on human behavior. The Aedes mosquito is predominantly a household mosquito and breeds in domestic environments and usually bites during the daytime.
Simple behavioral changes can dramatically reduce mosquito breeding:
Unfortunately, many people continue to view dengue prevention as the sole responsibility of city corporations. This mindset must change. Behavioral change communication should become a continuous national campaign.
Bangladesh must fully adopt integrated vector management (IVM) as the foundation of its dengue prevention strategy.
IVM is a comprehensive approach that combines:
Instead of conducting indiscriminate insecticide spraying, resources should be directed toward identifying mosquito breeding hotspots through entomological surveillance and geographic information system (GIS)-based mapping.
Integrated vector management also requires close coordination among the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, city corporations, municipalities, educational institutions, the Ministry of Local Government, the Department of Environment, and urban development authorities. Dengue is not simply a medical problem; it is an environmental and governance challenge.
No country has successfully controlled dengue without active community participation. Community engagement should move beyond awareness campaigns and evolve into community ownership. Neighborhood-based clean-up campaigns, school health programs, youth volunteer initiatives, and community surveillance teams can significantly reduce mosquito breeding sites.
A nationwide weekly "Dengue Clean Day" could become an effective public health intervention. Local communities should be encouraged to inspect their homes and surroundings regularly and report potential breeding sites to local authorities. Bangladesh's own dengue strategy recognizes community participation as the key to sustainable dengue control.
Rapid and often unplanned urbanization has transformed many areas of Bangladesh into favourable environments for Aedes mosquitoes. Blocked drainage systems, indiscriminate waste disposal, plastic containers, abandoned tires, rooftop water accumulation, and poorly managed construction projects continue to create ideal breeding habitats. Environmental sanitation should therefore become an integral component of dengue prevention.
Priority actions should include:
The responsibility for environmental sanitation extends far beyond the health sector. Urban planners, engineers, municipal authorities, construction companies, and communities must work together to reduce environmental risks. Bangladesh's current guidance specifically highlights waste management and sanitation as critical components of dengue prevention.
Every year, hospitals become overwhelmed when dengue cases begin to surge. This reactive approach must be replaced by proactive preparedness.
Institutional readiness should include:
Health facilities should begin preparing before the onset of the monsoon rather than waiting for patient numbers to increase. Early diagnosis and appropriate case management remain the most effective ways to reduce dengue-related deaths. These preparedness measures are also emphasized in national recommendations.
The World Health Organization (WHO) currently recommends the use of the dengue vaccine Qdenga® (TAK-003) for children aged 6-16 years living in areas with high dengue transmission intensity.
Importantly, vaccination should never replace traditional prevention measures. WHO clearly states that dengue vaccines should be implemented as part of a comprehensive dengue control strategy.
One of the most important lessons from recent dengue outbreaks is that surveillance systems must become more predictive.
Traditional case reporting alone is insufficient. Bangladesh requires an integrated early warning system that combines:
A modern surveillance system should identify high-risk areas before outbreaks occur rather than simply documenting cases after transmission has already intensified.
Effective surveillance can provide policy-makers with the information needed to deploy resources, strengthen vector control, and prepare health facilities in advance. National strategies already emphasize real-time reporting, hotspot mapping, and early warning systems.
Bangladesh continues to repeat the same mistake every year by initiating dengue control activities after the arrival of the monsoon. This approach must change. Seasonal preparedness should begin at least two to three months before the rainy season and include:
Dengue control activities should follow an annual preparedness calendar rather than an emergency response model. Current guidance recommends that control activities begin before the peak transmission season.
Bangladesh has successfully addressed many major public health challenges through strong political commitment and multisectoral collaboration. Dengue should be approached in the same way.
The country needs a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach that brings together:
The fight against dengue requires behavioral change, environmental responsibility, scientific surveillance, climate adaptation, institutional preparedness, and community ownership.
Dengue is no longer merely a seasonal outbreak. It is a warning signal about the intersection of climate change, urbanization, environmental neglect, and public health vulnerability.
Dr M Salim Uzzaman is a public health specialist & strategist (expert: EIDs, disease surveillance, One Health, and global health security).
The views expressed are personal.

item.title: Labuschagne makes the cut for Australia Test squad for South Africa. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Out-of-form Marnus Labuschagne can “still make a positive contribution”, chief Australia selector George Bailey said on Monday, after the struggling batsman was thrown a lifeline for the Test tour of South Africa.

Number three Labuschagne has failed to score a century since 2023, and flopped again in two home Tests against Bangladesh last month with scores of one, 31 and four.

He was subsequently axed from Australia’s squad for three One-day Internationals in Zimbabwe and another three in South Africa preceding the Tests.

But selectors opted against a red-ball change for what will be the team’s first Test series in South Africa since the infamous “Sandpapergate” ball-tampering scandal in 2018.

“(We’re) not shying away from the fact that we’d like some more runs from Marn… but we’re also confident that he can still make a positive contribution to that squad,” Bailey said.

“Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn’t been functioning as successfully as we would like.” Asked if the South Africa series would be Labuschagne’s last chance, Bailey dodged the question.
“No, I wouldn’t say that. But again, it’s a hypothetical, isn’t it?” he said.

Cooper Connolly, Matthew Kuhnemann and Michael Neser were also included in a 16-man squad which was otherwise unchanged form the last Bangladesh Test.

All-rounder Connolly’s selection is another indication that the 23-year-old is seen as a long-term prospect while Kuhnemann was preferred to Todd Murphy as the second spinner behind Nathan Lyon.

Neser, who like Labuschagne was born in South Africa, provides back-up for the pace trio of Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc.

Bailey said Connolly was primarily chosen for his batting, most likely as a middle order option but potentially as high as three.

“His overall development will continue to expand his ability to bat in a range of positions,” he said.

Australia travel to Durban for the first Test on October 9 before the series moves to Gqeberha and Cape Town.

Only Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood, Lyon, Steve Smith and Matt Renshaw survive from their last Test series in South Africa, when Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were all sent home in shame.

Smith was banned for a year and sacked as captain after conspiring to alter the ball using sandpaper during the third Test in Cape Town, while the now-retired Warner, considered the ringleader, was suspended for 12 months and stripped of all leadership roles.

Australia Test squad: Pat Cummins (captain), Scott Boland, Alex Carey, Cooper Connolly, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Matthew Kuhnemann, Marnus Labuschagne, Nathan Lyon, Michael Neser, Matthew Renshaw, Steve Smith, Mitchell Starc, Beau Webster

item.title: Makkah Defense Alliance: Should Bangladesh step into the quicksand?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
After World War II, military alliances emerged in various regions as a result of the ideological competition between the Western world and the Soviet Union. But in today’s world, there is no longer competition between two distinct camps, and many regions have no such military alliances.
That is perhaps why the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement has aroused curiosity in many countries. The geographical composition of the Makkah Alliance and the circumstances surrounding its formation have given rise to considerable speculation.
The formal journey of this alliance, comprising Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, began a month ago. On September 1, at the first formal meeting in Istanbul, it was decided to establish a secretariat in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia.
At the same time, the military and diplomatic leaders of the three countries decided to appoint a Pakistani official as the alliance’s first secretary general for a three-year term.
Following the political decision to form the alliance, the process of establishing its administrative and management structure is now beginning. The easier tasks will come first.
It is expected that the more complex steps required to make a military alliance effective will be taken in the future. However, beyond those complex steps, much remains to be determined -- including the alliance’s ideology, objectives, policies, expansion, and identification of enemies and allies.
It can be said that much more remains unknown about the alliance than is currently known. That is precisely why it has generated so much curiosity among countries outside the grouping.
At the Istanbul meeting, however, officials from the host country made some attempts to satisfy that curiosity, answering some, if not all, of the questions surrounding the alliance.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the alliance was created on the basis of international values such as respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states and non-interference in their internal affairs. However, declaring such values is far easier than adhering to them, as even a cursory look at world politics makes clear.
But there is little doubt that the issue of territorial integrity is of considerable importance to the alliance. Just as alliance member Turkey is fighting separatist Kurdish rebels in the southeast of the country, another member, Pakistan, is confronting increasing activity by independence-seeking armed groups in its Balochistan province.
Hakan Fidan said the Makkah Defense Alliance has no enemies and that its doors are open to other countries. “This alliance is not against any one country, and it is open to all those who share our values in our region,” he said.
Fidan said two things in a single sentence about the possible expansion of the alliance.
First, “open to all”, meaning anyone can join. This statement will give hope to those in Bangladesh who are interested in joining the alliance. Bangladesh has not yet been invited to join, but officials in Dhaka have been expressing their interest for several days.
But Fidan also added the words “in our region.” What exactly does he mean by “region” here?
The founding members of the alliance are primarily countries belonging to the West Asia-Persian Gulf-Mediterranean geopolitical space. Bangladesh, on the other hand, belongs to the South-Southeast Asia-Bay of Bengal region.
Regional media reports discussing potential new members of the alliance have more frequently mentioned Egypt and Syria. There is little doubt that Saudi Arabia is interested in bringing Egypt into the alliance, while Turkey wants to bring Syria under its umbrella.
It is difficult to identify any obvious role for Bangladesh in this Middle East-centred security and political framework.
Various local media reports suggest that there are concerns within the alliance about admitting new members. Any new member could bring additional military and political strength.
But it could also introduce different policy priorities, particularly in foreign affairs, as well as different security perspectives -- all of which could complicate the alliance’s operations.
For example, while Bangladesh could contribute experienced peacekeeping troops to the alliance, Dhaka’s geopolitical and strategic priorities would remain focused on Southeast Asia and the Bay of Bengal.
Bangladesh should aim to maintain cordial relations with all countries in West Asia. Participating in a military alliance in the region would mean becoming involved in local disputes, which would run counter to Bangladesh’s interests.
The debate in Dhaka over the alliance is also examining the India factor from two perspectives.
On the one hand, it is being argued that joining the alliance would strengthen Bangladesh’s security and deter India from aggression.
On the other hand, membership could have precisely the opposite effect.
Joining the alliance would mean establishing formal military ties with Pakistan, which could lead India to view Bangladesh as a threat to its security.
It is difficult to understand how a military alliance can be formed without identifying an “enemy.” No matter how “defensive” an alliance claims to be, why would three countries commit themselves to military action in one another’s defense unless they perceived a threat?
The question becomes even more relevant when one of the three countries possesses around 150 nuclear weapons.
The source of the threat has almost certainly been identified. But the secrecy surrounding it suggests that the alliance’s appeal and effectiveness could be undermined if that country or group were publicly named.
Fidan emphasized certain values in his speech, one of which was “non-interference in anyone’s internal affairs.” This principle was probably raised with Iran in mind.
Since the Islamic Revolution in Iran in 1979, the Gulf Arab countries have complained that Tehran seeks to export its revolution to Arab states. There is little doubt that Iranian revolutionaries wanted to overthrow the monarchical systems of the Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia.
Iraq invaded Iran in 1980 with financial and other support from Arab countries. Saddam Hussein believed that post-revolutionary Iran could be defeated easily. But after eight years of war, Iraq was forced to accept a ceasefire without achieving its objectives.
The question now is whether the Makkah Defense Alliance was created with Iran in mind. From the perspective of Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries, such an assumption would seem natural.
Although Pakistan maintains friendly relations with Iran, Islamabad has been providing troops for Saudi Arabia’s security for decades.
Turkey’s inclusion sends another message. Recent comments by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suggest that war between the two countries may only be a matter of time.
Turkey has been expanding its military presence and political influence in Syria over the past year and a half, developments that Israel views as a threat to its security.
Israel’s plan was to establish dominance across the region after destroying Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon, and the Assad regime in Syria. The final obstacle was Iran.
But the failure of the US war against Iran has almost derailed Israel’s plan. Israel is now focused on disarming Syria, but Turkey stands in the way.
The announcement of the alliance comes at a time when the security architecture of the Persian Gulf and eastern Mediterranean has almost collapsed.
The joint US-Israeli military operation aimed at overthrowing the Islamic regime in Iran has effectively failed, creating a security vacuum in the region.
Iran has shattered the perception that the US military presence in the Gulf guarantees the security of Saudi Arabia and other Arab monarchies.
There is considerable uncertainty over when, if ever, US military bases in the Gulf will return. It is believed that the Makkah Defense Alliance will attempt to fill this security vacuum.
The initial assessment is that the alliance is primarily focused on Iran and the Houthi group in Yemen. The main threats to Saudi Arabia’s security come from these two sources.
Israel had hoped to become the principal driving force behind a new regional security architecture following Iran’s defeat. Iran disrupted that plan by calling on Arab countries to coordinate their security with Tehran.
The Makkah Defense Alliance has created the possibility of a new geopolitical alignment in West Asia, in which a regional security architecture could emerge outside the orbit of the United States, Israel, and Iran.
Bangladesh’s ruling authorities probably believe that joining the alliance would not only strengthen the country’s economic interests, particularly manpower exports and energy imports, but also enable Dhaka to play a strategic role in this important region.
But are the interests and perspectives of the alliance’s founding members really the same? No. The same would apply to any new members.
The history of the Middle East teaches us that friendships and enmities rarely remain permanent. Loyalties can shift like the sands of the desert. Bangladesh will have to tread very carefully here, lest it stumble into quicksand.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster.
Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Chasing blue skies. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As the world marks the International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies, our country is confronted with a sobering truth: Our fight against air pollution is nowhere near where it needs to be.
Bangladesh continues to underestimate the deadly toll of polluted air, even as respiratory illnesses rise, premature deaths increase, and millions of people breathe toxic air every single day.
This day is meant to remind nations that clean air ought to be a fundamental right. For Bangladesh, it should serve as a wake‑up call.
Air pollution has long been one of our most pressing public health emergencies. We consistently rank among the world’s most polluted, with air in our capital and major cities far exceeding safe limits.
Yet, our national response remains fragmented, slow, and often reactive rather than preventive.
From children developing asthma at alarming rates to elderly citizens suffering from chronic diseases to workers needing to work while inhaling air thick with dust, smoke, and chemical emissions, air pollution affects every person but disproportionately affects the marginalized and vulnerable and moves us further away from becoming an equitable nation.
That illegal brick kilns and unregulated factories continue mushrooming is also among our biggest failures, all the while the true number of pollution‑linked deaths remains undercounted, masking the scale of the crisis.
To say we cannot continue down this path would be an understatement. Let today be a reminder that clean air is essential for economic growth, public health, and national stability.
The deadly toll of air pollution is rising, even if official numbers fail to capture its full extent. We must confront this reality with urgency and ambition and recognize that clean air is not a luxury but a necessity if we want to be a healthy, productive, and resilient nation.

item.title: Heeding the call for a liveable environment. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s latest remarks urging collective action for a pollution‑free Bangladesh must be heeded.
Pollution in our country, especially in our major cities, is a daily assault on public health, economic productivity, and the basic livability of our cities. As such, when the head of our government recognizes the issue and calls for unity and urgency, the nation collectively must listen and act.
Of course, our pollution crisis is multidimensional. We have already spoken of our struggling air quality in major cities that routinely falls into hazardous levels in our first editorial, but that is just one aspect of it.
Rivers are choked with industrial waste, sewage, and plastic. Noise pollution has become a constant urban stressor, and unplanned development continues to erode green spaces and natural buffers.
The consequences of this pollution are visible everywhere and affect everyone: rising respiratory illnesses, contaminated water sources, declining biodiversity, and a quality of life that is deteriorating even as the country strives for economic progress.
The prime minister is right to emphasize that this fight cannot be won by the government alone. Pollution is produced by factories that ignore regulations, by corporations that dump waste into canals, by unfit vehicles that belch smoke, and by institutions that treat environmental rules as optional.
A pollution‑free Bangladesh requires responsibility at every level, from policymakers to businesses to ordinary citizens.
A liveable Bangladesh must be the goal, and it is possible only if we treat pollution as the national emergency it is.

item.title: The great digital delusion. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
If you had told a Bangladeshi parent 20 years ago that their child would one day make millions of Taka a month by slapping dye into their hair, dancing wildly on a public overpass, or staging a screaming match with their in-laws in front of a ring light, they would have gently recommended a psychiatric consultation.
Yet, here we are in 2026.
The algorithm is the new deity, the smartphone is the altar, and "views" have somehow become a substitute for value.
Take, for instance, the recent domestic melodrama that dominated our feeds.
The internet exploded with details of infamous TikToker Prince Mamun allegedly joining forces with his second wife to physically assault and evict his own mother and mute sister from their home.
To complete this tragic soap opera, his former partner -- the ever-present "Blue Fairy" Laila -- rushed to the scene to offer shelter to the distressed mother, all under the piercing gaze of rolling smartphones and eager cameras.
Was it genuine heartbreak? Was it an orchestrated PR play? Does anyone even care anymore?
In the hyper-monetized content circus of Bangladesh, human dignity, filial piety, and familial trauma are no longer private matters.
They are mere "hooks" designed to drive retention rates, inflate impressions, and capture ad revenue.
When a society begins to trade its basic moral currency for digital validation, we must pause and ask: Is this truly the "future of work" we were promised?
There was a time when upward social mobility required sweat, late-night study sessions, and decades of professional discipline.
Today, creators like Prince Mamun, Opu Bhai, and Rakib Hossain have bypassed traditional educational paths entirely.
Armed with little more than raw charisma, sensationalism, and an uncanny ability to exploit digital algorithms, these individuals have accumulated fortunes that leave university graduates, engineers, and corporate executives scratching their heads in utter disbelief.
Seeing unlettered influencers pull in tens of thousands of dollars a month while a fresh graduate earns peanuts at an entry-level job has created a profound psychological rift among Bangladeshi youth.
Why endure 16 years of grueling academic pressure only to face a stagnating job market when you can buy a tripod, film a provocative vlog, and land a lucrative brand deal by next Tuesday?
Thousands of young Bangladeshis are abandoning classrooms and technical institutions, harbouring a dangerous ambition: To become "content creators."
They mistake temporary digital notoriety for a legitimate career, unaware that building a life on social media metrics is like building a house on shifting sand.
This entitlement to unearned wealth and status -- where one expects to enjoy all the rewards of social prominence without first putting in the sweat, integrity, or moral dues -- recently manifested in yet another grim headline.
Content creator Ripon Miah, who amassed nearly 1.9 million Facebook followers on the back of quick social media clips, was recently arrested by law enforcement after being accused of abusing his influencer status to harass and ultimately rape a 14-year-old schoolgirl in Netrakona.
Media reports revealed how local influential figures initially attempted to "settle" the heinous crime through an illegal local arbitration ( shalish ), fining him Tk5 lakh and asking him to leave the village while video clips of his apology went viral online.
Ripon’s trajectory -- from a local carpenter to a viral celebrity, and ultimately an accused predator attempting to buy his way out of criminal accountability with easy social media money -- serves as a chilling reminder of what happens when massive influence and financial windfalls precede character, discipline, and hard-earned merit.
It is the ultimate manifestation of wanting to pocket the rewards of success without paying the fundamental dues of human decency, rule of law, and honest labor first.
What these aspiring influencers fail to realize is that content creation is fundamentally unsustainable.
Relevance in the "reel-scrolling" era is ruthlessly ephemeral.
The same audience that elevates an influencer to digital royalty today will swipe away tomorrow without a second thought.
A single change in an algorithm, a shift in audience tastes, or a temporary suspension of monetization can instantly reduce a "social media millionaire" to complete financial oblivion.
Worse still, this desperate race for virality has given birth to a sinister, predatory ecosystem.
The promise of social media fame is no longer just a distraction -- it has turned into a dangerous trap.
Media reports across Bangladesh have documented tragic instances where young girls from vulnerable backgrounds were lured with promises of becoming "TikTok stars" or landed roles in viral videos.
Instead, they faced horrific fates -- abduction, sexual assault, and human trafficking networks operating under the guise of talent agencies and creator houses.
The tragic reality is that while a select few pocket cash from ad networks, scores of impressionable youths pay for this illusion with their lives, freedom, and dignity.
Even for those who manage to stay on the legitimate side of the law, the golden goose of online monetization is growing tired.
Platform giants like YouTube continuously refine their Partner Program policies.
In their ongoing efforts to appease advertisers, platforms are cracking down on repetitive content, sensationalized clickbait, low-effort clips, and ethical violations.
For Bangladeshi creators reliant on sensationalism or repurposed content, the revenue gravy train is slowing down.
While YouTube periodically adjusts regional monetization pathways, making it technically easier for localized content to earn revenue, the bar for qualifying content is rising sharply.
Algorithms are increasingly penalizing vulgarity, family drama, and synthetic outrage.
When the platforms decide to clean up their digital storefronts, hundreds of creators who traded their education for short-term views will find themselves with neither a steady paycheck nor transferable skills for the real world.
This brings us to an inescapable truth: Mobile-generated content can never ethically or practically replace real labour, technical expertise, and formal education.
A nation cannot run on reaction videos, pranks, and unboxing clips.
Who will design the bridges, manage the power grids, or write the software systems that keep our economy moving forward?
Who will treat the sick, harvest the crops, teach the next generation, or manufacture the very goods that influencers unbox on camera?
True labor builds tangible value. It instills discipline, produces tangible progress, and offers a level of personal self-respect that no amount of digital "likes" can ever match.
Formal and technical education are not merely decorative certificates but are the structural framework of a functional society.
They impart problem-solving capabilities, critical thinking, and resilient skills that withstand algorithmic shifts, economic downturns, and platform updates.
There is no shame in leveraging modern technology to express oneself, share stories, or build an audience.
But when content creation degrades into public spectacles of familial abuse -- where a mother's tears are treated as engagement fuel -- it ceases to be entertainment.
It becomes a sign of moral degradation masquerading as entrepreneurship.
We must strip away the illusion surrounding "influencer culture."
Let the youth enjoy their short-form videos, but let them also understand the clear line between a temporary hobby and a lifelong profession.
Real success is not measured in subscriber counts, brand deals, or viral scandals.
It is measured in the quiet dignity of honest work, the pursuit of real knowledge, and the enduring strength of human integrity.
In the end, when the screens go black and the servers shut down, it is honest, physical, and intellectual labor that will keep the world turning -- long after the last reel has been swiped away.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.
